questions.prompt: What does this Go program print?

query.explanation: Go integer division truncates toward zero, so -7/2 == -3, and the remainder takes the sign of the dividend: -7%2 == -1 (the identity a == (a/b)*b + a%b holds). Right shift of a signed value is arithmetic (sign-extending) and rounds toward negative infinity, so -7>>1 == -4, which differs from -7/2. Go has no unary bitwise-complement operator spelled '~'; it reuses the XOR operator '^' as a unary operator. For an unsigned type the complement wraps within the type's width: for uint8, ^60 == 255-60 == 195, never a negative number, because uint8 cannot represent one.
query.syntax:
a / b   // truncated toward zero
a % b   // sign follows dividend
a >> n  // arithmetic shift for signed types
^x      // unary bitwise complement
query.title: Go: integer division, remainder, shifts and bitwise NOT

questions.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a := -7
	var b uint8 = 60
	fmt.Printf("%d %d %d %d\n", a/2, a%2, a>>1, ^b)
}

choices.rationale: This assumes negative integer division and remainder round toward negative infinity, giving -7/2 = -4 and a remainder of 1. Go truncates the quotient toward zero, so a/2 is -3 and a%2 keeps the sign of the dividend: -1, as the output shows.

This treats a>>1 as identical to a/2 and so reuses -3. They are not the same for negatives: the arithmetic right shift keeps the sign bit and effectively floors, so -7>>1 is -4 while -7/2 truncates to -3, exactly the pair in the output.

This evaluates ^60 as if b were a signed int, giving -61. But b is declared uint8, so ^b stays uint8: the eight bits of 60 invert to 195. There is no implicit widening to int, and an unsigned type can never print a negative value.

questions.prompt: Which five lines does this program write to standard output?

query.explanation: Go's sized integer arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N with no overflow panic. int8(-100) + int8(-100) = -200, which wraps to -200+256 = 56. uint8(200) + 100 = 300 wraps to 300-256 = 44. Converting uint8(200) to int8 reinterprets the bits 0xC8 as -56. Go has no unary ~; unary ^ is bitwise complement, and for an unsigned 8-bit value it stays unsigned: ^uint8(200) = 255-200 = 55. The binary &^ is AND NOT (bit clear): 12 &^ 10 = 1100 &^ 1010 = 1100 & 0101 = 0100 = 4.
query.syntax:
x + y  // wraps mod 2^N for sized ints
^x     // unary bitwise complement
x &^ y // bit clear (AND NOT)
T(x)   // conversion reinterprets bits between same-size signed/unsigned
query.title: Sized integer wraparound, conversion, ^ and &^ in Go

questions.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var a int8 = -100
	var b int8 = -100
	var x uint8 = 200

	fmt.Println(a + b)
	fmt.Println(x + 100)
	fmt.Println(int8(x))
	fmt.Println(^x)
	fmt.Println(12 &^ 10)
}

choices.rationale: This assumes int8 and uint8 widen to a big int before arithmetic, so -100 + -100 stays -200 and 200 + 100 stays 300. Go keeps the operands' 8-bit type: the results wrap to 56 and 44, and int8(x) reinterprets the bits as -56, not 200.

Wrapping was applied to the sums, but int8(x) was read as a checked view that keeps the value 200, and &^ was treated as XOR (12^10=6). int8(200) reinterprets the byte as -56, ^x stays in uint8 giving 55, and 12 &^ 10 clears bits to 4.
Everything but line 4 matches, so ^x was computed as if x were a plain signed int: ^200 = -201. x is uint8, so ^ complements only its eight bits and the result is still uint8, printing 55.
